It's interesting when similar words have slightly different meanings in various languages. "Fanfara" in Polish means a short, musical flourish, usually performed on a trumpet, announcing something important - much like in English. However, Polish lacks the other meanings of fanfare in English: great attention to and interest in something or a showy outward display. "Fanfaronada" is a pejorative Polish term denoting boasting or obno×iousIy showing off one's bravery. @SBK in TO isn't the Autumnal Equinox on the 21st? If you're right, you better start advocating for calendars to move it to the correct day...

@Rachel This year, it's the 22nd but it does vary from year to year and depending where you live. Despite its name (equi + nox ➡️ equal + night, i.e., when day and night are equally long), it's based on the moment when the sun appears exactly above the equator. I don't know how much Al glop has infiltrated Britannica's website but here, for what it's worth, is their explanation. https://www.britannica.com/science/autumnal-equinox.

@Rachel  (& @SBK in TO)
Not only does the equinox occur on a specific date, but also a specific time, which varies from year to year. In 2026, it occurs on Wed., Sept 23 at 12:06am UT--"Universal Time," which used to be GMT, "Greenwich Mean Time." So, a couple minutes after midnight in Iceland and Morocco; but not in Greenwich, England, which follows Daylight Saving Time, so 1:06am there.
 
This means that, in eastern North America, it occurs this evening (Sept 22) at 8:06pm. But not all of eastern North America--in the Canadian Maritime Provinces (Atlantic Time), it occurs at 9:06pm. But not all of the Maritimes--New Brunswick doesn't observe DST, so for @JohnWM it occurs at 8:06pm. And then there's Newfoundland, where it occurs at 9:36pm. Does St. Pierre and Miquelon count as North America (10:06pm)? What about Greenland (11:06pm)?

To make things even more confusing, some of the sources I consulted said that this year, it occurs at five after the hour, and others at seven after.

So, @Rachel, it's possible that, in some years and in some locations, the autumnal equinox *could* fall on Sept. 21.

not noticing everyone else’s thumbs up.

The rest say together 

“Vad säger grisen?!”

That last person realizes now
they missed it and has to 

oink, nuff-nuff, or
